_comment: What a landing weight does to what it lands on. WORLD.md, locked: 'Weight
(Anchorite): ... Drop-forge -- crafting by crushing.'
The FOURTH use of one mechanism. The unraveling loosens, the Turning weathers,
attrition generalises, and this crushes -- same ConversionDef shape, same
StepTable, four different questions. This is the first of the four that is not
something the world does on its own: nothing here fires on a clock or a random
tick. Every rule waits for a player to lift something and let it go.
TWO ANSWERS, NOT A RECIPE LIST. The table answers one question -- what does this
do under force? -- and the world only has two answers. Rock SHATTERS: stone to
cobble to gravel to sand. Loose or soft matter PACKS: snow to ice to packed ice
to blue ice. A block does one or the other, never both, so the table can never
be read as 'crushing does whatever the designer wanted here'.
CHAINS, as everywhere else. Nothing arrives at its final state, so a player can
stop at any step and take the intermediate -- gravel is a destination, not a
stage on the way to sand.
'chance' is 1.0 throughout, and that is the difference between this table and the
three that run on their own. The unraveling and the Turning are weather: they
happen to a place over time, and a probability is how a rate is written. A crush
is an act. A weight that landed and did nothing 30% of the time would not read as
a rate, it would read as the spell being broken.
NOT here on purpose: anything a player builds out of. No bricks, no planks, no
worked stone, no glass. The Drop-forge is aimed by hand and ignores the claim
ledger by design -- see Crush -- so the only thing standing between it and a
misfire eating somebody's wall is that walls are not in this file. Ores are out
for a different reason: crushing an ore block into its mineral would make this
the best pickaxe in the game, and the spell is a workbench, not a mining rig.
